name: Clause-Analogue Construction

dimensions.form: A non-headed construction realized by one or more overt phrases, but with no VP and no constituent in Head function at the construction's own level
dimensions.meaning: A recoverable predication, situation, proposition, or speech-act update comparable to the interpretation of a Clause
dimensions.function: Construction-specific complement, adjunct, supplement, exclamation, echo, directive, or other stand-alone utterance
dimensions.distribution: Restricted to licensed non-verbal frames; it is not freely interchangeable with a Clause

1.definition: Conveys clause-like semantic or discourse content through a non-headed construction that is not a Clause
1.details: This node houses the constructions that CGEL calls verbless clauses while rejecting their assignment to the Clause category. Some have an overt subject-like expression plus a predicative expression (their hands above their heads; Dinner over); others consist overtly of a single NP, AdjP, PP, or predicative phrase whose subject or copular relation is recovered from the licensing construction or discourse (What a disaster!; No entry). The overt daughter phrases retain their own internal Heads, but none is Head of the higher clausal-semantics construction. Recovering an implicit predication or speech act in interpretation does not posit a silent VP in syntax.

examples.form: They stood with [their hands above their heads].
examples.note: Subject-like NP plus locative predicative, licensed as complement of with
Supplement with subject-like NP and predicative expression
Non-headed exclamative packaging with understood subject and copular relation
Non-verbal directive whose prohibition is supplied constructionally
Bare-predication polar echo with subject-like NP and predicative AdjP

constraints.description: No VP occurs in Head function; if the construction has a VP Head, it is a Clause instead.
Overt daughters may themselves be headed NPs, AdjPs, or PPs, but no daughter is Head of the higher clausal-semantics construction.
Clause-like content is recovered from the licensed construction and context; the analysis does not posit an unpronounced verbal Head.
Membership is construction-specific: an arbitrary non-verbal fragment does not automatically instantiate this construction.

projection.target: Recognizing the clause-analogue construction predicts recovery of an implicit predicational or speech-act relation and licensing in a delimited clause-like discourse or dependent function, while predicting the absence of verbal tense, auxiliary, and VP-complementation behavior
projection.evidence: CGEL documents recurrent, construction-specific correspondences between these non-verbal forms and finite or non-finite Clause interpretations across complements, supplements, exclamatives, echoes, and directives, even though this Constructionary draws the category boundary differently

grounds.note: The licensed non-verbal forms project recoverable predicational or speech-act content and restricted distributions
Documents recurrent form–interpretation pairings and their restricted complement, supplement, exclamative, and directive distributions

core.property: No Head at the construction's own level
diagnostics: no other daughter determines the construction's distribution
recognized supplement, echo, exclamative, or directive frame
NP/AdjP/PP utterance with conventional clause-like force

known_boundary_items: A Clause has a VP Head and is therefore formally disjoint from this construction
A headed NP or AdjP used merely as a referential fragment need not have clausal semantics
Coordination is also non-headed, but coordinate structure alone does not supply clausal semantics

curious.title: Sentence-like phrases with no verb
curious.summary: Some short phrases carry the meaning of a whole statement even though they contain no verb.
curious.body:
A notice reading No entry means something like "you may not enter." What a disaster! means something like "that's a disaster." Neither has a verb, yet we understand a full message. Dinner over, they resumed their game works the same way: it tells us the dinner was over.

This dictionary groups such phrases together. They get their clause-like meaning from the pattern they belong to and from the situation, not from a hidden verb. A clause here means a stretch of language built around a verb phrase, and these phrases aren't built that way. They also work only in particular frames, so an arbitrary scrap of words doesn't count.

examples.text: They stood with [their hands above their heads].

curious.try: Think of a sign or a short exclamation with no verb. What full sentence does it stand for?

teacher.summary: For advanced classes, verbless but clause-like utterances such as No entry and Dinner over.
teacher.explain: This dictionary groups together non-headed constructions with a clause-like interpretation but no VP in head function. CGEL calls these verbless clauses; this dictionary rejects that label, reserving Clause for structures with a VP head. Some have a subject-like expression plus a predicative expression (their hands above their heads; Dinner over). Others are a single NP, AdjP or PP whose subject or copular relation is recovered from the frame or the discourse (What a disaster!; No entry). This dictionary doesn't posit a silent verb: the implicit predication or speech act is recovered in interpretation, not supplied by an unpronounced VP. Membership is construction-specific, so an arbitrary non-verbal fragment isn't automatically included.
teacher.terms: CGEL: verbless clause. This dictionary: clause-analogue, kept separate from Clause because it has no VP head.

examples.text: They stood with [their hands above their heads].

watch_for: A learner might assume No entry has a hidden verb in the sentence's structure, when this dictionary says the meaning is recovered without positing one.
A learner might think any short fragment, such as a bare noun phrase naming something, carries clause-like meaning.
teacher.activity: Collect short verbless signs and exclamations from around the school. Students write the full-sentence meaning of each and say whether it's a command, a statement, an exclamation or a question.
